primaryText: They made John out (to be) a liar.
comment: A complex particle construction: a particle and an additional secondary predicate.

primaryText: They turned out (to be) intelligent.
They painted the barn up red.
They put the books down on the shelf.
They sent a schedule out to the stockholders.
comment: The dative PP is predicative, as chapter 3 argues.

primaryText: *What did they look [[the information about t] up]?
comment: Subextraction from the object NP is as bad as subextraction from small-clause subjects in general, (13b,c).

primaryText: *Who do they consider [[the brother of t] a fool]?
*What did they paint [[the door of t] black]?
*our looking of [[the information] up]
comment: Particle constructions resist nominalization like other small-clause constructions, (14b,c).

primaryText: *our consideration of [[John's brother] a fool]
*our painting of [[the door] black]
They made (*it) out that John is a liar.
comment: The finite clause is the complement of the ergative particle and stays in situ, so no dummy it appears; contrast (45).

primaryText: They find *(it) painful that John is a liar.
comment: The unergative adjective takes the clause as its external argument, which extraposes with dummy it.

primaryText: They made John out a liar.
*?They made out John a liar.
comment: SC2 is a barrier, so Case cannot reach its subject in situ and NP-movement is obligatory.

primaryText: *They made John a liar out.
They painted the barn up red.
*?They painted up the barn red.
*They painted the barn red up.
They made John out to be a liar.
(?)They made out John to be a liar.
comment: The infinitival marker to is prepositional, (58), so SC2 is no barrier and reanalysis licenses the in-situ subject.

primaryText: *They made John to be a liar out.
They put the books down on the shelf.
They put down the books on the shelf.
*They put the books on the shelf down.
They sent a schedule out to the stockholders.
They sent out a schedule to the stockholders.
*They sent a schedule to the stockholders out.
*What kind of a liar did they make out John t?
comment: Extraction of the predicate of SC2 fails whatever the particle's position: SC2 is a barrier and the particle no lexical governor.

primaryText: *What kind of a liar did they make John out t?
What kind of a liar did they make out John [to be t]?
comment: Subextraction from the predicate is governed by the copula.

primaryText: What kind of a liar did they make John out [to be t]?
On which shelf did they put down the books t?
comment: Verb-adjacent placement means reanalysis has applied, and the reanalysed verb-particle complex lexically governs the trace.

primaryText: *?On which shelf did they put the books down t?
comment: Somewhat less bad than (60b), and improved by an adverb after the particle (footnote 32).

primaryText: Which shelf did they put down the books [on t]?
Which shelf did they put the books down [on t]?
To whom did they send out a schedule t?
*?To whom did they send a schedule out t?
Who did they send out a schedule [to t]?
Who did they send a schedule out [to t]?
They carried up the hay onto the wagon green.
comment: The underlying order of the resultative predicate and the VP-adjoined adjectival small clause headed by green.

primaryText: They carried the hay up onto the wagon green.
They carried up the hay green onto the wagon.
comment: Extraposition of the predicate of SC2 is possible only with the particle adjacent to the verb, its trace being lexically governed after reanalysis.

primaryText: *They carried the hay up green onto the wagon.
John will bring up the rear.
comment: Verb-particle-object idioms with a fixed object have the inner order only, as expected if the object is generated as the particle's complement.

primaryText: The search party has given up all hope (of ...).
Jeremy put in a brief appearance.
She stood the fellow up.
comment: Outer-particle idioms leave the object unfixed: at S-structure it occupies the specifier of the small clause, the position of affected arguments, which idiom chunks cannot fill.

primaryText: He let the girl down.
John looked the information/it up.
*John looked up it.
comment: A weak pronoun cannot be Case-marked through the reanalysis chain, (163).

primaryText: John threw out THEM!
comment: A focally stressed pronoun is not weak and patterns with full NPs.

primaryText: John looked up him and her.
John dusted off that.
They put the books/them down on the shelf.
*They put down them on the shelf.

alternatives.form: They put down the books on the shelf.

comment: The ban on weak pronouns in the inner order carries over to complex constructions.

primaryText: They made John/him out to be a liar.
*They made out him to be a liar.

alternatives.form: They made out John to be a liar.

primaryText: They looked the information (right) up.
*They looked right up the information.
comment: Particle modification is impossible if verb-particle reanalysis has occurred, (169): incorporation cannot strand a bare modifier, (173).

primaryText: Han satte katten ned på gulvet.
comment: Constructed and judged by Arnfinn Vonen (fn. 37); Bokmål.

primaryText: Han satte ned katten på gulvet.
comment: Verb-adjacent placement is allowed, as in English (52b).

primaryText: *Han satte katten på gulvet ned.
comment: Clause-final placement is excluded, as in English (52c).

primaryText: På gulvet satte han ned katten t.
comment: The predicate of SC2 extracts when the particle is verb-adjacent, as in English (62a).

primaryText: *På gulvet satte han katten ned t.
comment: For many speakers the predicate of SC2 does not extract past an outer particle, as in English (62b).

primaryText: Hva satte han ned katten [på t]?
comment: Subextraction from the predicate of SC2 is perfect for all speakers whatever the particle's position, as in English (63).

primaryText: Hva satte han katten ned [på t]?
De sendte møteprogrammet ut til aksjonærene.
comment: The counterpart of English (53a).

primaryText: De sendte ut møteprogrammet til aksjonærene.
*De sendte møteprogrammet til aksjonærene ut.
Til aksjonærene sendte de ut møteprogrammet t.
comment: The counterpart of English (64a).

primaryText: *Til aksjonærene sendte de møteprogrammet ut t.
comment: The counterpart of English (64b).

primaryText: Hvem sendte de ut møteprogrammet [til t]?
comment: The counterpart of English (65a).

primaryText: Hvem sendte de møteprogrammet ut [til t]?
comment: The counterpart of English (65b).

primaryText: Ned på gulvet satte han katten.
comment: The particle and the transitive PP front together, as in English (39): they form a constituent.

primaryText: Ut til aksjonærene sendte de møteprogrammet.
*Vi har utsparka hunden.
comment: Overt incorporation of the particle is excluded in the active. Åfarli's example, Nynorsk; den Dikken cites his page 89.

primaryText: Vi har sparka ut hunden.
comment: Åfarli's example, Nynorsk; den Dikken cites his page 89.

primaryText: Vi har sparka hunden ut.
comment: Åfarli's example, Nynorsk; den Dikken cites his page 89.

primaryText: *Vi har avklipt tråden.
comment: Åfarli's example, Nynorsk; den Dikken cites his page 89.

primaryText: Vi har klipt av tråden.
comment: Åfarli's example, Nynorsk; den Dikken cites his page 89.

primaryText: Vi har klipt tråden av.
comment: Åfarli's example, Nynorsk; den Dikken cites his page 89.

primaryText: *Vi har bortkjørt avfallet.
comment: Åfarli's example, Nynorsk; den Dikken cites his page 89.

primaryText: Vi har kjørt bort avfallet.
comment: Åfarli's example, Nynorsk; den Dikken cites his page 89.

primaryText: Vi har kjørt avfallet bort.
comment: Åfarli's example, Nynorsk; den Dikken cites his page 89.

primaryText: Hunden vart utsparka.
comment: The passive counterpart of (134a): the particle may surface to the immediate left of the participle, which den Dikken analyses as overt syntactic incorporation. Åfarli's example, Nynorsk; den Dikken cites his page 89.

primaryText: Tråden vart avklipt.
comment: Åfarli's example, Nynorsk; den Dikken cites his page 89.

primaryText: Avfallet vart bortkjørt.
comment: Åfarli's example, Nynorsk; den Dikken cites his page 89.

primaryText: Hunden blev bortkörd.
comment: Swedish incorporates the particle overtly in passives only, like Norwegian; provided by Clas Garlén and Agneta Taube (fn. 59).

primaryText: Tråden blev avklippt.
Han lukkede katten ud.
comment: Danish particles normally follow their argument.

primaryText: *Han lukkede ud katten.
comment: The inner order is not found in Danish, which den Dikken records without deriving.

primaryText: Han opgav sine studier.
comment: Overt incorporation in an active clause, which Herslund observes is lexically conditioned and not a productive syntactic process (fn. 60).

primaryText: Han overtog forretningen efter sin far.
Han uddeler billeter.
Vi sparka ut hunden av huset.
comment: The inner order with av huset following shows that the noun phrase is the particle's complement and ut an ergative particle, which by UTAH carries over to English (147c). Åfarli's example, Nynorsk; den Dikken cites his page 83.

primaryText: Vi sparka hunden ut av huset.
comment: Åfarli's example, Nynorsk; den Dikken cites his page 83.

primaryText: *Jon sparka ut hunden døra.
comment: The cognate of English (147b) does not alternate; den Dikken leaves the reason open (fn. 70) and rejects Åfarli's Case Filter account of it (fn. 74). Åfarli's example, Nynorsk; den Dikken cites his page 83-84.

primaryText: Jon sparka hunden ut døra.
comment: Åfarli's example, Nynorsk; den Dikken cites his page 83-84.

primaryText: ?*Av huset sparket han (ut) hunden (ut)?
comment: Extraction of the constituent after the particle is impossible whatever the particle's position, as in English (152); fn. 73 notes that many speakers marginally accept the inner-particle variant with av hvilket hus and contrast it with the outer one. Judgments collected by Alma Næss; Bokmål.

primaryText: *Døra sparket han hunden ut?
comment: The noun phrase after the outer particle in (150) cannot be extracted, so it is not the particle's Case-marked complement (fn. 74). Judgments collected by Alma Næss; Bokmål.
